title: Cyclophilin A stabilizes the capsid protein p72 to facilitate African swine fever virus replication

paper_content.abstract: African swine fever virus (ASFV) is a large DNA virus that poses a major threat to the global swine industry. Its virion is encapsulated by an icosahedral capsid predominantly composed of the structural protein p72, which constitutes approximately one-third of the total virion mass. Despite its abundance, the mechanisms regulating p72 stability remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that host-mediated stabilization of p72 is essential for efficient ASFV replication. Mass spectrometry of p72 co-precipitates identified host cyclophilin A (CypA, also known as PPIA) as a key binding partner of p72. CypA interacts with p72 both in vitro and in vivo, specifically engaging exposed regions of p72 via its hydrophobic cavity. CypA interaction stabilizes p72 by reducing its ubiquitination and preventing proteasomal degradation, whereas cyclic CypA inhibitors destabilize p72 by disrupting this interaction and promoting its ubiquitination. Importantly, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of CypA markedly impairs ASFV replication. Mechanistically, CypA inhibition disrupts viral factory formation and virion assembly by decreasing p72 protein accumulation without affecting its transcription. Together, our findings uncover a host-dependent mechanism regulating capsid protein stability and highlight host CypA as a promising target for antiviral strategies against ASFV.
paper_content.introduction:
African swine fever (ASF) is currently the most devastating infectious disease affecting swine, causing substantial economic losses worldwide1, 2. It is characterized by high morbidity and mortality rates (reaching up to 100%) in both domestic and wild pigs, and is designated as a notifiable disease by the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH)3. First reported in Kenya in 1921, ASF has since spread globally over the past century, affecting numerous countries and regions4. Despite its severe impact, there are currently no safe and effective vaccines or antiviral therapeutics commercially available for its prevention or treatment, posing significant challenges to ASF control.

ASF virus (ASFV), the causative agent of ASF, is a large double-stranded DNA virus with a complex icosahedral architecture5. ASFV particles, approximately 200 nm in diameter, consist of multilayered structures, including a genome-containing nucleoid, core shell, inner envelope, icosahedral capsid, and an external lipid envelope6. The most abundant component of the ASFV virion is the major capsid protein p72, which constitutes about 33% of the total mass of the virion7. p72 has been well-demonstrated to play a critical role in capsid formation and viral assembly8-11, suggesting that viral or cellular factors regulating p72 may affect ASFV infection. Previous studies have shown that the ASFV-encoded protein pB602L functions as a chaperone facilitating p72 folding12, 13. Repression of pB602L expression results in the decreased p72 protein levels and the formation of aberrant zipper-like structures instead of icosahedral ASFV particles14. In contrast, p72 degradation is essential during the early phase of ASFV replication, driving capsid disassembly and enabling the release of core particles containing the viral genome into the cytoplasm following fusion of the viral inner envelope with host endosomal membranes, thereby facilitating viral DNA delivery into host cells15, 16. These findings suggest that p72 must be precisely and temporally regulated throughout the ASFV life cycle, likely through host factors that stabilize p72 during later stages of infection. Despite its essential role in virion assembly, the mechanisms governing p72 stability remain largely unknown.

CypA is abundantly expressed and possesses chaperone-like and prolyl isomerase activities that modulate protein folding and function, thereby influencing diverse biological processes, including MAPK signaling, RIG-I pathway, and cytokine production17-19. It has also been implicated in pathogen infections and a wide range of disease processes18. Whether CypA plays a role in ASFV infection remains unclear.

In this work, we identify host CypA as a critical regulator of p72 stability and ASFV infection. Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) combined with mass spectrometry reveals a specific interaction between CypA and p72, which is further characterized by AlphaFold3 structural modeling, mutagenesis, and binding assays. CypA interaction protects p72 from K63-linked ubiquitination-mediated degradation, whereas inhibition or depletion of CypA accelerates p72 turnover, impairing viral replication. Furthermore, CypA inhibition disrupts viral factory formation and impedes virion assembly by reducing p72 protein accumulation during ASFV infection. These findings uncover a host-dependent mechanism controlling p72 stability and suggest that targeting the CypA-p72 interaction could represent a potential antiviral strategy.
paper_content.results:
Host CypA is a potential binding partner of the ASFV p72 protein
As the major component of the ASFV capsid, the viral p72 protein — encoded by the B646L gene — plays a critical role in ASFV virion assembly8, 11. It is well-established that B646L transcription initiates at 5 ~ 6 h post-infection (hpi) and is progressively upregulated during the late stages of ASFV infection, displaying a distinct expression pattern compared to the early genes CP312R and CP204L (encoding p30)20. In this study, porcine alveolar macrophages (PAMs) were infected with the genotype II ASFV HLJ/18 strain (referred to as ASFV unless otherwise noted), and samples were harvested at various time points post-infection for Western blot analysis to examine the expression kinetics of these viral proteins. Consistent with the transcriptional data20, p72 protein levels markedly increased at the later stages, in contrast to the early expression of CP312R and p30 (Fig. 1A). Given that protein abundance is controlled by multiple interconnected processes, including mRNA transcription, post-translational modifications, and protein degradation21, it is plausible that the accumulation of p72 at the late-stage of ASFV replication is also regulated by certain host factors after its synthesis. However, the mechanisms governing the stability of p72 protein in host cells remain largely unknown.

To explore potential mechanisms regulating p72 stability, we first sought to identify host factors that interact with p72. ASFV-infected PAMs were subjected to a co-IP with an anti-p72 antibody. As expected, viral p72 was specifically enriched by the anti-p72 antibody but not by the control IgG (Fig. 1B). The resulting co-precipitates were then analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), which identified a porcine cyclophilin-derived peptide, “FDDENFILK” (Fig. 1C). This peptide showed strong signal intensity in the p72-enriched sample but was absent in the IgG control (Fig. S1A). Sequence alignment of porcine cyclophilin family members revealed that both CypA (PPIA) and PPIE contain this peptide (Fig. 1D), suggesting p72 may associate with either or both proteins. Because cyclophilin family members share high sequence similarity22, we conducted GST pulldown assays using recombinant GST-tagged porcine cyclophilins and lysates from HEK293T cells expressing p72 to preliminarily assess their interactions. While most cyclophilins showed weak p72 binding, CypA and PPIE exhibited the strongest and comparable ability to recruit p72 (Fig. S1B). To determine the predominant binding partner, we examined the subcellular distributions of p72, CypA, and PPIE. Whereas p72 was mainly cytoplasmic and PPIE was strictly nuclear, CypA was present in both cytoplasm and nucleus (Fig. 1E), indicating that CypA, but not PPIE, has the spatial basis to interact with p72 in the cytoplasm. Together, these results suggest that host CypA may serve as a major binding partner of p72.

CypA is highly conserved across humans and animal species, including Ornithodoros, exhibiting approximately 100% identity between Sus scrofa and Phacochoerus africanus (warthog) (Fig. 1F). Emerging evidence suggests that CypA modulates the stability of different viral proteins, such as the HIV capsid23, the poxviruses C6 protein24, and the SARS-CoV-2 spike25. Therefore, it is reasonable to speculate that host CypA may likewise regulate p72 stability, warranting further investigation.

CypA interacts with viral p72 protein both in vitro and in vivo
To confirm the interaction between CypA and p72, we performed a series of binding experiments. Recombinant Strep-tagged trimeric p72 protein (referred to as recombinant Strep-p72) (Fig. S2) purified from yeast was subjected to Strep pulldown assays with GST or GST-CypA obtained from E. coli. We found that GST-CypA, but not GST alone, was efficiently recruited by Strep-Tactin resin with the recombinant Strep-p72 (Fig. 2A). In contrast, in the absence of recombinant Strep-p72, Strep-Tactin resin did not capture GST-CypA (Fig. 2B), which indicates that it is p72 that directly interacts with CypA in vitro. Moreover, co-IP in HEK293T cells co-expressing Strep-p72 and CypA-HA revealed that p72 was specifically detected in the CypA-enriched precipitates (Fig. 2C), confirming the formation of CypA-p72 complex in cells. Thus, these results demonstrate that CypA binds to ASFV p72 in vitro and in vivo.

Since intracellular co-localization is often a prerequisite for protein-protein interactions, we further examined subcellular co-localization of CypA and p72. Consistent with Fig. 1E, in plasmid-transfected HEK293T cells, Strep-p72 predominantly localized in the cytoplasm, whereas CypA-HA was present in both the cytoplasmic and nuclear regions (Fig. 2D). Importantly, co-expression of Strep-p72 and CypA-HA in HEK293T cells revealed strong cytoplasmic co-localization of these two proteins (Fig. 2D, E). We further assessed the dynamics of this co-localization in PAMs during the course of ASFV infection. At 6 hpi, only a small fraction of PAMs expressed low levels of p72, which localized to a restricted cytoplasmic region without detectable co-localization with CypA (Fig. 2F). However, as the infection progressed, p72 accumulated and showed pronounced cytoplasmic co-localization with endogenous CypA, particularly within viral factories (Fig. 2F). This co-localization was initially observed at 12 hpi, persisting to 24 hpi. A weaker p72 signal in factories was observed in a small fraction (~10%) of infected cells at late stages, potentially reflecting extensive p72 accumulation and redistribution. Importantly, the production of infectious progeny virions was initiated at 12 hpi and increased over time (Fig. 2G), coincided temporally with CypA-p72 co-localization, suggesting a potential role of CypA in promoting efficient virion assembly. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that host CypA co-localizes with ASFV p72 in host cells, likely contributing to viral replication.

CypA binds to the exposed regions (ERs) of p72 through its hydrophobic cavity
Prompted by the above interaction data, we sought to explore the binding mode between CypA and p72. While the structure of human CypA has been extensively characterized26, 27, the porcine CypA structure remains unresolved. Using the AlphaFold3 server, we predicted the structure of porcine CypA, which displayed a high similarity to its human counterpart (Fig. 3A), consistent with their high sequence identity (Fig. 1F). Given the demonstrated accuracy of AlphaFold3 in modeling biomolecular interactions28, we employed it to predict the CypA-p72 binding complex. Considering that p72 exists as a large trimer (~219.5 kDa) and CypA is a relatively small protein (~17.8 kDa), we hypothesized that the p72 trimer may bind CypA at a molar ratio of 1:3. The AlphaFold3-predicted model of a p72 trimer complexed with three CypA molecules exhibited high confidence (pTM = 0.74), with each CypA molecule binding to p72 in an identical fashion (Fig. 3B). Further detailed inspection of the binding interface using PyMOL29 revealed that CypA likely interacts with the apical exposed regions (ERs) of p72 via its 33 amino acid residues (spanning positions 54 ~ 153) (Fig. 3C, D). Notably, the interaction interface includes multiple residues (R55, F60, M61, Q63, A101, F113, W121, L122, and H126) of the hydrophobic cavity of CypA (Fig. 3D), suggesting that this hydrophobic pocket may be essential for p72 binding.

To experimentally verify this prediction, we generated a series of CypA truncation mutants with sequential deletions of 20, 40, 60, or 80 amino acids from either the N- or C-terminus (Fig. 3E). These mutants were expressed in E. coli, purified, and subjected to in vitro binding assays with the recombinant Strep-tagged p72 trimers. Deletion of 20 or 40 residues from either terminus had no significant effect on the binding between CypA and p72. However, removal of 60 or 80 residues from either end nearly abolished the interaction (Fig. 3F). As shown in Fig. 3E, deletions of 60 or more residues from either terminus disrupted key elements within the hydrophobic cavity (spanning residues 54 ~ 126), thereby impairing its structural integrity. To directly examine the role of the hydrophobic cavity in p72 binding, we generated a CypA(8A) mutant in which all key residues within the cavity were substituted with alanine (Fig. 3G). This mutant showed a marked loss of p72-binding capacity (Fig. 3H). These results support our structural prediction, confirming that the hydrophobic cavity of CypA serves as the primary binding region for p72.

We next sought to validate the corresponding CypA-binding site on p72. Previous structural studies have shown that p72 monomer adopts a double jelly-roll fold with four exposed regions (ERs) or insertions8, 9, 11. In our earlier study, we generated five porcine monoclonal antibodies (B1, F11, C9, H3, and G6) targeting p72 and determined their complex structures with p7213. Comparative analysis revealed that the binding epitopes of four of these antibodies (B1, F11, C9, and H3) significantly overlapped with the predicted CypA-binding region, all of which are located in the ERs of p72; Notably, each p72 trimer is capable of simultaneously binding three antibody molecules (Fig. 3I). In vitro binding assays confirmed that these four p72 antibodies effectively competed with CypA for p72 binding, supporting the idea that p72 recruits CypA via its ERs (Fig. 3J, K). In contrast, antibody G6, which binds the central apical region of the p72 trimer at a 1:1 ratio, failed to compete with CypA for p72 binding, similar to the negative control anti-p30 antibody (Fig. 3J, K). Given that the four competing antibodies (B1, F11, C9, and H3) all targeted ER1 on the outer apex of p72, while the non-competing G6 did not bind ER1 (Fig. 3I), we propose that the critical amino acid residues mediating p72-CypA interaction are primarily located within ER1. Collectively, our findings indicate that the CypA-p72 interaction is mediated through the hydrophobic cavity of CypA and the ER1 region of p72, laying a foundation for further elucidating how CypA may modulate p72 stability.

CypA stabilizes viral p72 by reducing its K63-linked ubiquitination
ASFV p72 has been reported to undergo degradation in host cells15, 30. To elucidate the major pathway responsible for p72 degradation, we treated p72-expressing cells with different inhibitors. While the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 (BafA1) induced LC3-II accumulation, it had minimal impact on p72 protein levels (Fig. 4A). In contrast, treatment with MG132, a classical proteasomal inhibitor, not only enhanced Ub conjugation but also markedly increased p72 accumulation (Fig. 4A), indicating that p72 degradation is predominantly mediated by the proteasome. Furthermore, the stability of p72 was also significantly promoted by TAK-243 (MLN7243) (Fig. 4A), a first-in-class UBE1 inhibitor31 that depletes cellular polyubiquitin chains. Thus, the ubiquitin-proteasome system is primarily responsible for p72 degradation in host cells. Notably, the ASFV pB602L protein is essential for the correct folding and trimer assembly of p72, and the expression of p72 alone leads to the formation of misfolded p72 aggregates11, 12, 14. To further investigate the regulation of pB602L on p72 stability, we co-expressed p72 and pB602L in cells and conducted inhibitor treatment assays. Consistent with the results above, we observed similar effects of the inhibitors on p72 stability when the experiments were performed in the presence of pB602L (Fig. 4A). These findings indicate that the ubiquitin-proteasome system serves as the primary pathway for p72 degradation, irrespective of the presence or absence of pB602L.

It is noteworthy that co-expression of pB602L upregulated p72 protein levels (Fig. 4B), in agreement with a previous study14. Given that CypA has been reported to regulate the stability of several viral proteins24, 25, 32, we examined its potential role in modulating p72 levels. Similar to pB602L, CypA expression increased p72 protein levels (Fig. 4B and Fig. S3A). To ensure physiological relevance, p72 was co-expressed with pB602L in all subsequent experiments, unless otherwise specified. Notably, CypA exhibited a dose-dependent effect in enhancing p72 accumulation in cells (Fig. 4C), highlighting its critical role in regulating p72 expression or protein stability. However, CypA co-expression did not change the mRNA level of p72 (Fig. 4D), which indicates that CypA probably regulates the protein folding or stability of p72. Notably, while pB602L promoted p72 trimer formation regardless of CypA expression, CypA alone failed to induce trimerization (Fig. S3B), indicating that CypA does not exert a chaperone-like function in p72 folding. Deletion of endogenous CypA in cells resulted in a decreased p72 protein level, whereas re-expression of CypA restored p72 accumulation (Fig. 4E), further supporting its regulatory role in maintaining p72 stability. To assess p72 degradation rate, we used cycloheximide (CHX) to block protein synthesis and found that CypA expression suppressed p72 degradation (Fig. 4F). These results suggest that CypA enhances p72 protein stability in cells.

Since p72 was reported to undergo ubiquitination-mediated degradation30, we investigated whether CypA affects p72 ubiquitination. To this end, p72 was enriched from cells expressing p72 alone or co-expressing p72 and CypA under denaturing conditions, and its ubiquitination levels were analyzed. While strong ubiquitination of p72 was detected in the absence of CypA, co-expression of CypA markedly reduced its ubiquitination (Fig. 4G, H and Fig. S3C). To further characterize the ubiquitin (Ub) linkage type, cells were co-transfected with p72 and HA-tagged wild-type Ub or a series of Ub mutants, each retaining a single lysine residue at the indicated position. This analysis revealed that p72 is predominantly modified by K63-linked polyubiquitin chains in cells (Fig. 4I, J). Notably, overexpression of CypA resulted in a pronounced reduction of K63-linked polyubiquitination on p72 (Fig. 4K). Although K63-linked ubiquitination is typically associated with signal transduction33, 34, several studies have demonstrated that it can also target substrates for degradation35-37, and a recent study specifically implicated K63-linked ubiquitination in promoting p72 degradation30. Together, these findings suggest that CypA enhances protein stability of p72 by suppressing its K63-linked ubiquitination.

CypA inhibitors destabilize p72 by disrupting CypA binding and enhancing p72 ubiquitination
Cyclosporine A (CsA), a cyclic undecapeptide with the highest known binding affinity for CypA, is a well-characterized CypA inhibitor17, 38. CsA is an immunosuppressive agent derived from fungi, whereas its non-immunosuppressive analogs, such as NIM811 and Alisporivir (Debio-025), have been developed as therapeutic alternatives39. Structural studies have resolved the complexes formed between CypA and these cyclic undecapeptide inhibitors40-42, revealing that their binding sites overlap with the p72-binding surface of CypA (Fig. 5A). This structural overlap suggests that CsA and its analogs may disrupt the interaction between CypA and p72. To test this, we performed an in vitro binding assay using the recombinant Strep-p72 and GST-CypA proteins in the presence or absence of CypA inhibitors. As shown in Fig. 5B, the addition of CsA to the in vitro binding system effectively blocked the binding of CypA to p72. Similarly, NIM811 and Alisporivir also inhibited CypA-p72 binding (Fig. 5B), confirming that these inhibitors can competitively interfere with this interaction. Since these cyclic undecapeptide inhibitors occupy the hydrophobic cavity of CypA43, 44, these findings further support that p72 engages this same hydrophobic pocket, reinforcing the conclusion that CypA binds p72 through its hydrophobic interface.

Given that CypA enhances p72 stability, we hypothesized that inhibitors interfering with this interaction could destabilize p72. To investigate this, p72-expressing cells were treated with CypA inhibitors for 24 h and p72 protein levels were analyzed by Western blot. CsA treatment induced a dose-dependent reduction in p72 protein levels (Fig. 5C, E), with noticeable effects starting from 5 μM and a maximal reduction at 20 μM. NIM811 similarly decreased p72 levels in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 5C, D). A CHX chase assay further demonstrated that NIM811 accelerated p72 degradation, shortening the time for the protein intensity to reach 50% of its initial value from 6 h to 2.95 h (Fig. 5F, G). Moreover, analysis of p72 ubiquitination in the cells treated with CypA inhibitors revealed that CsA or NIM811 exhibited a robust ability to increase the ubiquitination of p72 (Fig. 5H, I and Fig. S4), in contrast to the reduction induced by CypA overexpression (Fig. 4K). Together, these findings establish that the cyclic peptide inhibitors of CypA promote p72 degradation by enhancing its ubiquitination.

Inhibition of CypA impairs ASFV infection
The data described above suggest that CypA may play a critical role in ASFV infection. To investigate this, we performed viral infection assays using BK2258 cells, a wild boar-derived cell line known to support ASFV replication45. BK2258 cells were engineered to stably express either a control sgRNA (Ctrl-sg) or CypA-targeting sgRNAs (CypA-sg) via the CRISPR/Cas9 system. Western blot analysis confirmed that CypA protein expression was efficiently ablated in CypA-sg cells (Fig. S5A). Upon ASFV infection, CypA-sg cells exhibited a marked reduction of viral p30 expression compared to control cells (Fig. S5A). Quantitative PCR (qPCR) further revealed that loss of CypA significantly impaired the production of extracellular ASFV virions in the supernatants (Fig. S5B). To validate these findings in a primary cell context, PAMs were transfected with either CypA-targeting siRNAs (siCypA-1/2/3) or a negative control siRNA (NC) prior to ASFV infection. Similarly, CypA knockdown led to substantial reduction in both viral protein expression and ASFV replication in PAMs (Fig. 6A, B). These results indicate that CypA is essential for the efficient ASFV infection.

Since cyclic peptide inhibitors of CypA destabilize p72, we next examined whether these inhibitors could impact ASFV infection. PAMs were infected with ASFV in the presence of CypA inhibitors, including CsA, NIM811, and Alisporivir. All three inhibitors significantly decreased virions production in the supernatants of infected cells (Fig. 6C). Western blot analysis revealed that treatment with these compounds decreased the intracellular accumulation of viral proteins (Fig. 6D), and immunofluorescence staining showed a marked decrease in the number of p72-positive cells in the inhibitor-treated groups (Fig. 6E). To further quantify the infection ratio, we employed an artificially attenuated ASFV strain, HLJ/18-7GD, which expresses the fluorescent markers EGFP and mCherry46. CsA and NIM811 caused reduction in fluorescent signals in the infected PAMs (Fig. 6F), in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. S5C, D). Flow cytometry analysis corroborated these findings, showing that treatment with CypA inhibitors decreased the proportion of the infected cells by approximately tenfold or more (Fig. 6G, H and Fig. S5E). Consistently, Western blot analysis revealed a dose-dependent suppression of p72 and p30 expression in the infected PAMs by CypA inhibitors (Fig. 6I, J and Fig. S5F), and qPCR quantification of extracellular virions in the cell supernatants confirmed a dose-dependent inhibitory effect of CypA inhibitors on ASFV infection (Fig. 6K, L and Fig. S5G). Notably, these CypA inhibitors had minimal effects on cell viability at the indicated concentrations (Fig. S6A, B). Collectively, these results demonstrate that CypA inhibition, either through genetic decrease or pharmacological intervention, effectively suppresses ASFV infection.

Cyclic undecapeptides targeting CypA suppress ASFV replication kinetics
To evaluate the impact of CypA inhibition on ASFV replication kinetics, PAMs were treated with CypA inhibitors and infected with ASFV HLJ/18-7GD strain. The infected cells, which express fluorescent signals, were monitored and collected at different time-points for analysis. At 12 and 24 hpi, fluorescence intensities remained comparably low in both the DMSO-treated control and inhibitor-treated groups (Fig. 7A, B). However, as ASFV infection progressed (48 hpi late), fluorescence intensity in the control group increased substantially, indicating robust viral replication, whereas only a modest increase was observed in the inhibitor-treated groups (Fig. 7A, B). Consistently, multistep growth curve analyses showed that CypA inhibitors markedly reduced infectious virion replication, especially during the later stages of infection (Fig. 7C, D). Together, these findings demonstrate that cyclic peptide inhibitors of CypA effectively impair ASFV replication dynamics.

We next assessed the expression of viral proteins p72 and p30 during ASFV infection. Treatment with CsA or NIM811 markedly inhibited the time-dependent accumulation of both viral proteins (Fig. S7A, B), suggesting that CypA inhibition may finally interfere with the expression of viral genes. To investigate the effect of CypA inhibitors on viral gene transcription further, RNA-seq analysis was performed on NIM811-treated or untreated PAMs, with ASFV infection at 72 hpi (Fig. S7C, D). In line with previous studies20, 47, more than 160 viral genes were highly expressed in ASFV-infected cells (Fig. 7E). However, NIM811 treatment obviously reduced the levels of the viral gene transcription (Fig. 7E and Fig. S7E, Supplementary Data 1). qRT-PCR analysis of CP204L (p30) and B646L (p72) mRNA levels further confirmed that although viral gene transcription was elevated at 48 hpi and much higher at 72 hpi, this transcriptional activity was significantly suppressed by CypA inhibitors (Fig. 7F, G). These results demonstrate that CypA inhibitors can impair the transcription of viral genes during multi-cycle replication.

ASFV infection is known to induce hemorrhagic fever, accompanied by exacerbated inflammatory responses in multiple organs, ultimately causing pig mortality48. To determine whether CypA inhibitors can mitigate ASFV-induced host inflammation, we conducted host transcriptomic analyses of the infected PAMs. ASFV infection upregulated numerous host genes (Fig. S8A, Supplementary Data 2), many of which are associated with inflammatory pathways, including cytokine receptor signaling and the PI3K signaling pathway (Fig. S8B, Supplementary Data 3). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed significant activation of inflammation-related processes and notable alterations in plasma membrane components following ASFV infection (Fig. S8C, Supplementary Data 4). Notably, volcano plot analysis showed that NIM811 treatment effectively suppressed the ASFV-induced upregulation of host gene expression (Fig. S8A), a finding further supported by heatmap analysis (Fig. S8D, Supplementary Data 5). Collectively, these data suggest that CypA inhibition not only disrupts ASFV replication but also attenuates virus-induced inflammatory responses, highlighting the therapeutic potential of cyclic peptide inhibitors of CypA as antiviral agents against ASFV replication.

Inhibition of CypA impairs viral factory formation and virion assembly by reducing p72 protein levels
Because viral adsorption, internalization, uncoating, biosynthesis, assembly, and budding are essential steps in the ASFV life cycle49, 50, we next investigated which of these processes are regulated by CypA. To this end, BK2258 cells expressing either Ctrl-sg or CypA-sg were used to evaluate the effect of CypA on ASFV adsorption and internalization. Comparable levels of adsorption and internalization were observed in both cell lines, independent of CypA expression (Fig. 8A). Similarly, treatment of PAMs with the CypA inhibitors CsA or NIM811 did not significantly affect viral adsorption or internalization (Fig. 8B), indicating that CypA primarily modulates post-entry steps during ASFV infection.

To define the specific stages controlled by CypA, we conducted single-cycle ASFV replication assays in PAMs and collected samples over time to monitor viral DNA replication, as well as the mRNA and protein levels of B646L (p72). As shown, viral DNA replication in a single-cycle infection was not significantly affected by CsA or NIM811 (Fig. S9A). Transcription of B646L began to increase significantly at 8 hpi, peaked at 12 hpi, and remained at high levels thereafter, with no significant differences between inhibitor-treated and control groups (Fig. 8C). In contrast, Western blotting revealed that p72 protein was markedly reduced upon treatment with CsA or NIM811, whereas in control group, p72 became detectable at 8 hpi and accumulated progressively over time (Fig. 8D, E and Fig. S9B). Notably, the levels of another viral protein, p30, were unaffected by CypA inhibition (Fig. 8D, E). These results demonstrate that CypA primarily regulates p72 protein levels, rather than broadly influencing viral genome replication or early viral gene expression.

Given that certain viral proteins, including p72, help retain structural proteins within the assembly area and thus contribute to ASFV virus factory organization14, 51, we next asked whether CypA inhibition disrupts this process. BK2258 cells were subjected to immunofluorescence staining for p72 and p54, the latter serving as a marker for viral factory localization52. Treatment with CypA inhibitors markedly reduced p72 signals and disrupted the formation of p54-positive puncta (Fig. 8F). Confocal microscopy further revealed that large cytoplasmic viral factories co-stained with p54 and DAPI were present in DMSO-treated cells, whereas inhibitor-treated cells exhibited substantially smaller factories (Fig. 8G, H), indicating compromised viral factory formation and impaired virion assembly. To directly assess virion assembly, we examined ASFV-infected PAMs treated with DMSO or CypA inhibitors by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Numerous mature icosahedral virions were readily observed within viral factories in DMSO-treated control cells (Fig. 8I, J). In contrast, CypA inhibitor-treated cells contained markedly fewer mature virions and exhibited obvious aberrant tubular structures in viral factories (Fig. 8I), partially resembling previously reported zipper-like assemblies induced by disruption of p72 or pB602L14, 53. Consistently, CypA deficiency also promoted the formation of aberrant structures in viral factories of ASFV-infected cells (Fig. S9C). Together, these findings demonstrate that CypA inhibition disrupts ASFV viral factory organization and virion assembly by destabilizing p72 protein, thereby impairing ASFV infection.

Facility and Ethics Statements
All experiments involving live ASFVs were conducted in the enhanced biosafety level 3 (P3+) facility at the Harbin Veterinary Research Institute (HVRI), Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (CAAS), with approval from the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs of China. All animal experiments were approved by the Committee on the Ethics of Animal Experiments of the HVRI, CAAS (Approval number: 250417-01-GR), and were performed in accordance with institutional guidelines.

Cell and viruses
Primary porcine alveolar macrophages (PAMs) were isolated from 5-week-old healthy specific-pathogen-free (SPF) Landrace piglets, regardless of sex, as previously described79, 80, and were maintained in RPMI-1640 medium (Gibco, #C11875500BT) supplemented with 20% porcine serum (HyClone, #SH30908.04), 100 U/mL penicillin and 100 μg/mL streptomycin (Gibco, #15140122), and 2 mmol/mL glutamine at 37 °C with 5% CO₂ in a humidified incubator. The wild boar kidney cell line (BK2258), human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T, CRL-3216, ATCC), and human cervix epithelial HeLa cells (CCL-2, ATCC) were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Gibco, #C1 1995500BT) containing with 10% Fetal bovine serum (FBS; Sigma, #F8687-500mL) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin at 37 °C with 5% CO₂. For transfection experiments, cells were transfected using Lipo293 (Beyotime, #C0521), lipofectamine 2000 (Life Technologies, #11668019), or polyethylenimine (PEI; Polysciences, #23966-100), according to the manufacturer's instructions. The wild-type, virulent genotype II ASFV strain HLJ/18, previously isolated from domestic pigs, and the artificially attenuated strain HLJ/18-7GD were maintained in our laboratory46, 80.

Plasmid construction
The gene encoding porcine CypA (Uniprot: P62936; NM_214353.1) was amplified from PAM cDNA and cloned into pCDNA3.0 for mammalian expression and into pGEX-4T-1 for bacterial expression. The ASFV B646L gene encoding p72 (GenBank: QBH90570.1) and the B602L gene encoding pB602L (GenBank: QBH90568.1) were also cloned into the pCDNA3.0 for mammalian expression. Truncated variants of CypA and other porcine cyclophilins were generated by PCR and inserted into pGEX-4T-1 for recombinant expression and purification in E. coli. BL21 (DE3).

Antibodies and reagents
The anti-p72 rabbit polyclonal antibody, anti-p72 mouse monoclonal antibody, anti-p30 mouse antibody, anti-p54 antibody, and anti-CP312R mouse antibody were generated in-house, which are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. Mouse monoclonal antibodies against Flag (#L-MAb03), HA (#L-MAb01), and GST (#L-MAb04) were obtained from Biolinkedin (Shanghai). Alignment of amino acid sequences
Gene sequences of porcine cyclophilins, including CypA/PPIA (NM_214353.1), PPIB (XM_021093880), PPIC (XM_003129041), PPID (NM_001244386), PPIE (XM_013999195), PPIF (XM_001929483), PPIH (XM_003128098), and PPIL1 (XM_003128368), were retrieved from NCBI. Gene or protein sequences of CypA orthologs from human (NM_021130.5), monkey (NM_001032809.1), cattle (NM_178320.3), dog (XM_038689274.1), cat (NM_001009370.1), chicken (NM_001166326.2), mouse (NM_008907.2), rabbit (NM_001082057.1), Phacochoerus africanus (warthog, XP_047619276.1), and Ornithodoros turicata (XP_064487992.1) were also obtained from NCBI. Amino acid sequences were translated from coding sequences (CDS) of genes using SnapGene software (Dotmatics, available at https://www.snapgene.com). Multiple sequence alignment was performed with MUSCLE algorithm81.

Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP)
Co-IP assays were conducted using ASFV-infected PAMs or HEK293T cells co-transfected with Strep-tagged p72 and HA-tagged CypA for 36 hours. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 500 g for 5 minutes and lysed in Co-IP buffer consisting of 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, and 1× protease inhibitor cocktail. Lysates were subjected to ultrasonication using a non-contact automated ultrasonic disruptor (5 seconds on, 8 seconds off, for 60 cycles). After centrifugation at 12,000 g for 20 minutes at 4 °C, the clarified supernatants were incubated overnight at 4 °C with either anti-p72 or anti-HA antibodies for immunoprecipitation. Immune complexes were washed five times with Co-IP buffer, resuspended in 1× SDS loading buffer, and boiled at 100 °C for 30 minutes prior to analysis by Western blotting.

Mass spectrometry analysis
Mass spectrometry analysis was performed on control IgG- and anti-p72-enriched samples (one biological replicate each) from PAM lysates, following previously described procedures with minor modifications82, 83. Protein bands were excised from SDS-PAGE gels and subjected to in-gel digestion. Gel pieces were destained with 30% acetonitrile in 50 mM NH₄HCO₃, reduced with 10 mM dithiothreitol at 56 °C for 30 min, and alkylated with 60 mM iodoacetamide in the dark for 30 min. After dehydration, samples were rehydrated with sequencing-grade trypsin (Promega) in 50 mM NH₄HCO₃ and incubated overnight at 37 °C. Peptides were sequentially extracted with 60-90% acetonitrile containing 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid, dried, and desalted on C18 columns. The resulting peptide samples were redissolved with 0.1% formic acid and analyzed by liquid chromatography (LC) using an UltiMate3000 Rapid Separation system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to a Q Exactive HF-X Orbitrap (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated in data-dependent acquisition (DDA) mode. Raw MS data were processed with MaxQuant (v2.7.5.0)84 using default and specified parameters, including trypsin digestion allowing up to two missed cleavages, variable modifications of methionine oxidation and protein N-terminal acetylation, and the use of both unique and razor peptides for protein quantification. MS tolerances were set to 20 ppm for FTMS precursors and 0.5 Da for ITMS fragments. Peptide-level false discovery rate (FDR) was set at 1%, with a minimum peptide length of seven amino acids. Database searches were performed against both the Sus scrofa reference proteome (UPE000008227) and the ASFV HLJ/18 strain proteome (GenBank: MK333180.1).

Expression and purification of recombinant proteins
Recombinant Strep-tagged p72 trimer protein was expressed and purified in yeast cells as previously described85, 86. For bacterial expression of GST-tagged proteins, pGEX-4T1 plasmids containing full-length CypA or its truncation constructs were transformed into E. coli BL21 cells. Transformed bacteria were first grown on LB agar plates containing 100 µg/mL ampicillin at 37 °C. A single colony was then picked and cultured in 5 mL LB medium with shaking at 220 rpm overnight. In the next day, the culture was inoculated into 500 mL fresh LB medium and grown at 37 °C for 2~3 h, until the OD600 reached 0.6~0.8. Protein expression was induced by adding IPTG to a final concentration of 0.5 mM, followed by incubation at 16 °C overnight. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 5,000 g for 10 min, washed once with PBS, and resuspended in NETN buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.6), 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% TritonX-100, 1 mM EDTA, 2 mM PMSF, and 1 mM DTT. Cell lysis was performed using a high-pressure cell disruptor. After centrifugation at 12,000 g for 30 min at 4 °C, the supernatant was collected and incubated with Glutathione Sepharose 4B beads for 2 h at 4°C with gentle rotation. After washing five times with NETN buffer, GST-tagged proteins were eluted using freshly prepared elution buffer containing 200 mM Tirs-HCl (PH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, and 50 mM reduced glutathione. Eluted proteins were dialyzed overnight at 4°C in 2 L of dialysis buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.6), 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM DTT, and 20% glycerol. After dialysis, proteins were aliquoted and stored in -80 °C refrigerator. Protein purity and concentration were assessed by SDS-PAGE followed by Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining.

Strep pull-down assay
Recombinant GST or GST-tagged proteins, Strep-tagged p72 trimer, Strep-Tactin resin, and a protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche) were combined into 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes. The mixtures were supplemented with co-IP buffer (50 mM Tris, pH 7.6; 150 mM NaCl; 1% TritonX-100; 1× protease inhibitor cocktail; 0.5% Micrococcal Nuclease (M0247S); 1mM CaCl2; and 2 mM DTT) to a final volume of 800 µL. For competitive binding assay, 5 µM cyclic undecapeptide CypA inhibitors or 10 µg p72-specific antibodies were added to the reaction. The samples were incubated at 4 °C for 4 h or overnight with gentle rotation. After incubation, the Strep-Tactin resin was collected by centrifugation at 500 g for 1 min and washed five times with pre-chilled co-IP buffer. The bound proteins were eluted by mixing the resin with 1× SDS loading buffer and boiling at 100 °C for 30 min. Samples were subsequently analyzed by Western blotting.

Immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy
Immunofluorescence was performed to analyze the subcellular localization of the indicated proteins, as previously described87. PAMs or HeLa cells were seeded in 12-well plates containing sterile glass coverslips and infected with ASFV or transfected with the indicated plasmids for 24 h. Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 10 min and permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 20 min at room temperature. After three washes with PBS (10 min each), cells were blocked in 1 % BSA in PBST (PBS containing 0.1% Tween-20) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary antibodies diluted in the blocking buffer were applied to the cells and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The following day, cells were washed three times with PBST and incubated with the appropriate fluorescently labeled secondary antibodies (1:1000 dilution in blocking buffer) for 1 h at room temperature. After three additional washes with PBST, nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (0.2 μg/mL) for 20 min. Coverslips were then washed, mounted onto glass slides using fluorescence mounting medium (Dako Omnis, #NS3023), and allowed to air-dry overnight in the dark. Fluorescence images were acquired using a standard fluorescent microscope or a Zeiss LSM 800 confocal microscope.

Cycloheximide (CHX) chase assay
Transfected or inhibitor-treated cells were exposed to CHX (100 μM) for the indicated time periods, followed by Western blot analysis of p72. Band intensities were quantified using Adobe Photoshop and normalized to the corresponding loading control (if needed) and to the initial time point (t = 0) of each group. As the normalized intensity-time data displayed an approximately linear decline, the degradation rates were determined by performing a simple linear regression in GraphPad Prism (version 9.5.0). The rate of linear decrease was obtained from the slope of the fitted linear equation Y = slope × X + b, where b represents the initial intensity at t = 0. For clarity, we report the estimated time required for the intensity to decrease to 50% of the initial value, calculated as t50% = b/ (2 × |slope|).

In vivo ubiquitylation assay
In vivo ubiquitination was performed as previously described88, with minor modifications. Cells expressing Strep-p72, with or without CypA co-expression or CypA inhibitor treatment, were harvested by centrifugation at 500 g for 5 min, washed once with PBS, and resuspended in 100 µL TSD buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl; pH 7.6; 2 % SDS; and 5 mM DTT). Samples were boiled at 100 °C for 30 min, then centrifuged at 12,000 g for 10 min. The supernatants were collected and diluted 10-fold with co-IP buffer to reduce the SDS concentration from 2% to 0.2%. Diluted lysates were incubated with 20 µL Strep-Tactin resin at 4 °C overnight with gentle rotation. The resin was washed five times with cold co-IP buffer and boiled in 1× SDS loading buffer. Precipitated proteins were analyzed for Western blot analysis using anti-ubiquitin or other indicated antibodies.

Gene knockdown by siRNA transfection
Three siRNAs targeting Sus scrofa CypA (GenBank: XM_021078519.1) and a non-targeting control siRNA (NC) were synthesized by GENCEFE Biotech (Wuxi, China):
(1) siCypA-1: Forward: GGUUCCUGCUUUCACAGAATT;
Reverse: UUCUGUGAAAGCAGGAACCTT;
(2) siCypA-2: Forward: GGGCAUGAAUAUUGUGGAATT;
Reverse: UUCCACAAUAUUCAUGCCCTT;
(3) siCypA-3: Forward: CUGACUGUGGACAAAUCUATT;
Reverse: UAGAUUUGUCCACAGUCAGTT;
(4) NC: Forward: UUCUCCGAACGUGUCACGUTT;
Reverse: ACGUGACACGUUCGGAGAATT.
PAMs were seeded in 12-well plates and incubated for 6 h prior to transfection. Cells were transfected with 80 pmol of siRNA per well using the Gencefe Super Trans transfection reagent (GENCEFE Biotech) and incubated for 12h. Following transfection, the medium was replaced with fresh complete growth medium, and cells were cultured for an additional 36 ~ 48 h. Subsequently, cells were infected by ASFV at a MOI of 0.2 and incubated for 72 h. After infection, culture supernatant was collected for viral DNA quantification, and cells lysates were prepared for Western blot analysis.

Construction of CypA-deficient cell lines by CRISPR/Cas9 system
CypA-deficient HEK293T cell line was generated using the CRISPR/Cas9 technology, as described previously25. Briefly, three sgRNA sequences targeting the human CypA gene (NM_021130.5) were designed using the CRISPOR online tool (http://crispor.tefor.net/) and cloned into the lentiCRISPRv2 vector (Addgene, #52961) following the standard procedures89. HEK293T cells were seeded into 6-well plates and cultured overnight. Cells were then co-transfected with packaging plasmid psPAX2 (Addgene, #12260), envelope plasmid pMD2.G (Addgene, #12259), and the lentiCRISPRv2-sgRNA plasmids at a ratio of 2.5:1:3.5. After 48~72 h, lentivirus-containing supernatant was collected and filtrated through 0.45 μm filters. For transduction, 2 mL of viral supernatant was mixed with 2 mL of fresh complete growth medium containing 10 μg/mL polybrene and added to target cells in 6-well plates. After 24 h, the medium was replaced with fresh growth medium, and cells were cultured for an additional 24 h. Cells were then passaged into 10-cm dishes and cultured in medium containing the appropriate antibiotic for at least five passages to enrich for transduced populations. To isolate knockout clones, cells were sorted by flow cytometry into 96-well plates (one cell per well). Clones were screened by Western blot using anti-CypA antibody, and successful knockout clones were further confirmed by gene sequencing.

A similar strategy was used to construct CypA-deficient BK2258 cells. Three sgRNA sequences targeting the Sus scrofa CypA gene (XM_021078519.1) were designed using CRISPOR and cloned into the lentiCRISPRv2 vector. Lentiviral particles were produced as described above and used to transduce BK2258 cells. After 48 hours, transduced cells were selected in antibiotic-containing medium for at least five passages and assessed for CypA knockout by Western blotting.

The sgRNA sequences used in the study were as follows:
(1) Human CypA sgRNAs25: 5’- CTTGGGCCGCGTCTCCTTTG -3’;
5’- TTCTTCGACATTGCCGTCGA -3’;
5’- ATCCTAAAGCATACGGGTCC -3’.
(2) Porcine CypA sgRNAs: 5’- GCGATGTCGAAGAAGACGGT -3’;
5’- TCGAAGGAGACGCGGCCCAA -3’;
5’- AACTTCCGTGCTCTGAGCAC -3’.
(3) Non-targeting control sgRNA: 5’- ACGGAGGCTAAGCGTCGCAA -3’.

ASFV infection assay
The ASFV infection procedure was performed as described before45, 90, 91, with minor modifications. PAMs or BK2258 cells were seeded in 12 well-plates and cultured for 6 h or 12 h prior to ASFV infection. Cells were then incubated with ASFV at the indicated multiplicity of infection (MOI) at 37 °C for 2 h. Cells were washed three times with PBS and maintained in culture medium containing 20 % porcine serum (for PAMs) or 3% FBS (for BK2258) in a 5% CO2 incubator at 37 °C. At the indicated time points, both supernatants and cells were collected for further analysis. ASFV genomic DNA was extracted from supernatants using QIAamp® DNA Mini Kits (Qiagen, Germany) and quantified by quantitative PCR (qPCR) using an ABI QuantStudio5 system (Applied Biosystems, USA) with primers targeting the B646L gene. Infected cells were processed as followed: fixed in 4% PFA for immunofluorescence staining; harvested in 1× SDS loading buffer for Western blot analysis; or lysed in TRIzol reagent for total RNA extraction and subsequent gene expression analysis.

Virus adsorption and internalization assays
ASFV binding and internalization assays were performed as previously described92. For the adsorption assay, BK2258 stable cell lines or PAMs treated with CypA inhibitors were incubated with ASFV (MOI = 5) at 4 °C for 2 h to allow viral binding. Unbound virions were removed by washing the cells five times with ice-cold PBS. Cells were then harvested for total DNA extraction, followed by qPCR quantification of ASFV genomic DNA. For the internalization assay, BK2258 cells or PAMs were first incubated with ASFV (MOI = 5) at 4 °C for 2 h to enable viral attachment. After five washes with ice-cold PBS, cells were shifted to 37 °C and incubated in growth medium for an additional 2 h to facilitate viral internalization, in the presence or absence of CypA inhibitors. The cells were then incubated with trypsin-EDTA for 2 min at 37 °C to remove noninternalized particles. Cells were then collected for total DNA extraction and qPCR analysis of internalized ASFV genomes.

Flow cytometry analysis
PAMs were seeded in 12-well plates and cultured for 6 h prior to infection with ASFV HLJ/18-7GD (MOI = 0.1) for 72 h, in the presence or absence of CypA inhibitor treatment. Infected cells were either examined by fluorescent microscopy or analyzed by flow cytometry. For flow cytometry analysis, cells were harvested by trypsinization, neutralized with complete medium, washed with PBS, and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Single-cell suspensions were prepared by passing the cells through a 70-μm cell strainer. Cells were first gated on forward scatter (FSC-A) versus side scatter (SSC-A) to exclude debris and cell aggregates. mCherry-positive infected cells were subsequently identified by gating on mCherry fluorescence versus SSC-A, using uninfected cells as the negative control. Data were acquired on a flow cytometer and analyzed using FlowJo software (v10.8.1).

RNA sequencing and bioinformatic analysis
PAMs were infected with or without ASFV (MOI = 0.1) for 72 h in the presence or absence of NIM811. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent, and high-throughput RNA sequencing was performed by BMKgene. Raw FASTQ files from RNA sequencing were quality-filtered using fastp93, followed by alignment to the reference genome using HISAT294. Gene-level counts were quantified with featureCounts95, and differential expression analysis was conducted using DESeq2 package96, applying thresholds of |log2(Fold change)| ≥ 2 and adjusted p-value ≤ 0.01. Functional enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was performed using clusterProfiler R package97, with reference to the Gene Ontology98 (GO: https://www.geneontology.org) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes99 (KEGG: https://www.genome.jp) pathway databases.

Quantitative RT-PCR analysis
Total RNAs were extracted from ASFV-infected PAMs using TRIzol reagent, and RNA concentrations were measured with a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. A total of 1 μg RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using the PrimeScript™ RT reagent Kit with gDNA Eraser (Perfect Real Time) (#RR047A, Takara). Quantitative PCR was performed in triplicate in a 96-well plate using 50 ng cDNAs per well, the SYBR® Green Realtime PCR Master Mix (TOYOBO, #QPK-201), and an ABI QuantStudio5 system. Relative gene expression levels were calculated using the 2(–ΔΔCt) method, with GAPDH as the internal reference. The PCR primers used were: ASFV B646L (forward: 5′-ACGGCGCCCTCTAAGGGT-3′; reverse: 5′-CATGGGCAGCTTCAAACGTTTC-3′) and pig GAPDH (forward: 5′-ACCCAGLAAGACTGTGGATGG-3′; reverse: 5′-ACGCCTGCTTCACCACCTTC-3′).

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
PAMs were infected with ASFV (MOI = 5) for 24 h in the presence or absence of CypA inhibitor treatment. Infected PAMs were harvested and fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde in PBS (PH 7.4) at 4°C overnight. Fixed samples were then dehydrated through a graded ethanol series, embedded in epoxy resin, and processed for ultrathin sectioning and staining according to standard protocols. Sections were examined using a Hitachi H-7650 transmission electron microscope (Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan) operated at 80 kV. Digital images were captured and analyzed using Adobe Photoshop.

Statistics and reproducibility
Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Unless otherwise stated, all experiments were independently repeated at least three times with similar results, and representative images are shown. Statistical significance between groups was determined using two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test or ordinary one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons test, as indicated in the figure legends. All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (version 9.5.0).

Data availability
The mass spectrometry data generated in this study have been deposited in the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the iProX partner repository under accession code PXD073232 [https://proteomecentral.proteomexchange.org/cgi/GetDataset?ID=PXD073232]. The RNA-seq data generated in this study have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession code GSE300823 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE300823]. The previously published PDB structures referred to in this study include 3K0N [https://www.rcsb.org/structure/3K0N], 1CWA [https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1CWA], 1CWM [https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1CWM], and 5HSV [https://www.rcsb.org/structure/5HSV]. All data are available within the Article, Supplementary Information, or Source Data file. Source data are provided with this paper.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript the authors investigate the interaction of the African swine fever virus p72 major capsid protein with cyclophilin A (CypA). Although CypA has previously been shown to have important and diverse roles during replication of several other viruses. This is the first study to describe a role for CypA during replication of ASFV. CypA was one of the main proteins the authors detected by mass spectrometry in co-precipitates by an antibody against p72 from ASFV infected porcine alveolar macrophages. Subsequently this interaction was confirmed by direct binding between the tagged recombinant proteins and by coprecipitation following transient expression in transfected cells. The interaction of CypA with p72 was mapped to exposed regions on p72 and a sequence of CypA spanning a cavity region. Interaction of CypA was shown to reduce K63 linked ubiquitination of p72 and proteasomal degradation. Inhibitors of CypA reduced the size of virus factories and resulted in aberrant assembly of virions thus reducing virus replication kinetics. The authors indicate this interaction as a promising target for antiviral drug development against ASFV. The manuscript provides interesting novel data on an ASFV host interaction to stabilise the p72 capsid protein hence enhancing virus replication. The experiments are generally comprehensively carried out and clearly described and results support the conclusions drawn.
Specific Points:
1. As described by the authors, the p72 protein assembly into trimers which are incorporated into the virus capsid requires the virus encoded B602L chaperone although this protein isn’t incorporated into virus particles. Without co-expression of the B602L p72 is not expressed in the native trimeric form. To obtain recombinant p72 protein the authors express p72 with or without B602L in yeast. Although this co-expression with B602L has previously been shown to produce the native trimeric form of p72 in this manuscript the data to confirm this is achieved in the current study is not presented. The authors should present this data to confirm that the recombinant p72 used in experiments is assembled into trimers and that the monomeric form of p72 is absent. This data is important for the interpretation of experiments shown in Fig 1, and S1.
2. One important question, which is not fully resolved in this study, is the stage of replication when p72 is associated with CypA. The authors data suggest this interaction is important during virus assembly most likely after the assembly of the trimeric form of p72. In Figure 2 F immunofluorescence images from ASFV infected porcine alveolar macrophages fixed at 24 hpi infection at high multiplicity of infection are shown. Staining with anti-p72 and anti-CypA shows co-localization across the cytoplasm although not in factory structures which at this stage seem largely devoid of either DNA or p72 protein. At this late stage of infection it would be expected that progeny infectious virions have been produced some and would be moving to the cell surface or already been released. This data seems to suggest that CypA colocalises with virions as they move to the cell surface and even in projections from the cell, suggesting a possible role for the interaction of CypA with virions after virus assembly. To better understand the role of the CypA interaction with p72 the authors should repeat this experiment at different time points after infection. A parallel time course of infectious virus titre would establish when progeny virions are produced. This analysis may also help to establish if the CypA remains associated with p72 in the virus factories, no CypA is detected in the factories in the image shown in Fig 2F at this time point (24 hpi).
3. In Figure 6 the authors use Western blotting to measure accumulation of protein p30, a protein expressed from early times, during ASFV infection rather than p72 which is expressed from later times and is incorporated into virions. The authors should explain the reason why Western blotting with anti-p72 isn’t used in these experiments as Western blotting against both p30 and p72 is used in Fig 7 C. If both were used consistency between experiments would be better.
4. In Fig 7 ASFV replication kinetics are compared in CypA inhibitor treated and non-treated cells by several assays including measurement of numbers of fluorescent cells, expression of proteins by Western blotting, global transcription of ASFV genes, genome copy numbers. The impact of the treatment on the infectious virus titres are not shown. These data should be included to support the claim by the authors that treatment with drugs targeting CypA may be an effective antiviral treatment.
5. Figure 9 shows a cartoon to summarise the results from the study. This is helpful although some points haven’t been established or are confusing. The diagram shows the interaction between p72 and CypA in the cytoplasm but not in the virus factory whereas as discussed in point 2 above this hasn’t been established in the current study. Indeed the data shown in Fig 2F suggest CypA may be associated with migrating virions. In addition transcription of the mRNA for B646L appears to be shown outside the factory whereas the late transcription is assumed to be inside the factory where the replicating genomes are accumulated.
Minor Points:
1. In the text and Figure 1 legend the numbers of replicates of the co-precipitation and mass spectrometry analysis is not given.
2. Legend Figure 4A states that p72 was expressed in the presence or absence of B602L. On the figure the label shows B602L was included in all of these experiments.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Zhao and colleagues present data to characterize the interaction between ASFV p72 with cyclophilin A which was discovered by AP-MS. Truncation experiments and use of inhibitors allowed to narrow down the interacting site. Function of CYPA with respect to ASFV replication are tested with infection experiments using PAM and genetically engineered knock-out BK2258 porcine cells. The main findings are that CYPA interacts with p72, stabilizes it against proteasomal degradation and enhances ASFV infection. These findings are important in the ASFV field however interactions of CYPA with matrix proteins of other viruses have been described before.
The subject of the study is of great importance as ASFV threatens the pig industries almost worldwide. The manuscript is well written. However, some of the presented data needs more explanation and experimental confirmation, for details please see the section with the ‘Minor points’. Also, some figures seem overcrowded and could be rearranged and greater care should be taken to give appropriate references for all tools that were used, some are mentioned in this section.
The presented data is interesting but also raises questions. In a number of experiments the authors describe the negative effect of CYPA loss or inhibition on the expression of ASFV proteins, which can be explained by the decreased number of cells infected in the inoculated cell batch (see Figure 6). Protein expression data on single cell basis are not presented, but Figure 8 shows an obvious reduction of ASFV particles within an infected cell in the absence of CYPA suggesting lower expression of at least structural proteins. It remains unclear why successful internalisation of ASFV leads to low level infection in only very few cells in the absence of CYPA while viral entry is not affected (Fig 8). Unfortunately, this crucial experiment (adsorption / internalisation) is not described precisely, no reference is given, and no controls are used (if available at all). The manuscript would also improve if the authors added some information from the literature about the impact of CYPA on a number of cellular processes that may, in addition to the described interaction with p72, influence the outcome of an ASFV infection (MAPK signalling, RIG-I IFN, regulation of cytokines) in the Introduction section.
Minor points

Line 137: Fig 2 shows localisation of both proteins in the cytoplasm which explains the overlap but does not prove the interaction, pls correct. The magnification of Fig 2D,F is too low to draw this conclusion.
Line 150: pls add a reference for PyMOL

Figure 1D: what is the coloring based on?
Figure 4F: the band intensities for WT and KO cells are very different, I find it hard to judge if the degradation is really ‘accelerated’ based on the very different starting levels.
Fig 4G: these diffuse bands are hard to interpret, pls add a quantitation of the experiment.
Fig 4H: the conclusion is difficult to follow without quantitation of the bands including a correction for the input of Ub. Pls avoid ‘above’ for references within the manuscript but specify in detail how the blots were done. The lower HA panel has 9 tracks, all others have 10, pls correct.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this study, Kong et al identify cyclophilin A (CypA) as a host interacting partner of the African swine fever virus (ASFV) major capsid protein p72. Their findings suggest that p72-CypA interaction prevents proteosome-mediated degradation of p72, thereby facilitating viral replication. Conversely, suppression of CypA expression or treatment with CypA inhibitors significantly impairs viral replication, highlighting a novel potential therapeutic target against ASFV.
While the work presents novel and intriguing data, the effect of CypA suppression and CypA inhibitors on viral assembly contradicts previous evidence on the consequences of p72 knockdown and needs clarification. Furthermore, key aspects of CypA's mechanism of action on p72 stability remain unclear and would require further investigation.
Major points:
- Inconsistencies in ASFV assembly defects. The reported effects of CypA inhibitors on viral assembly do not align with established phenotypes resulting from p72 abrogation. Previous studies (e.g., Ref. 9) have shown that suppression of p72 expression leads to the massive formation of aberrant viral structures known as “zippers” in viral factories, resulting from the co-assembly of unprocessed polyproteins pp220 and pp62 with inner envelope precursors. Similar structures are observed when the viral chaperone pB602L is abrogated, which blocks p72 trimerization (Refs. 11 and 13). Surprisingly, these hallmark features are absent in the presence of CypA inhibitors, and this discrepancy is not addressed in the manuscript. Instead, CypA inhibitors reduce viral factory size—an effect more suggestive of compromised formation of ER-derived viral membrane rather than decreased p72 levels.
These discrepancies raise questions about whether CypA inhibitors specifically act only through modulation of p72 degradation, or whether they impact additional viral components or replication stages. To clarify this, it would be highly informative to examine the ultrastructure of viral factories following CypA knockdown or knockout. If similar effects to those of the inhibitors are observed, off-target or broader effects should be considered to account of the effects of CypA abrogation and inhibitors.
Does CypA solely regulate p72 stability? The data do not conclusively demonstrate that CypA’s only role is in stabilizing p72, since most infection experiments were conducted at low MOI (0.1–1 PFU) and analyzed at late post-infection times (72–96 hpi), allowing for multiple replication cycles. To unravel primary from secondary effects, it would be beneficial to re-analyse the impact of CypA silencing and CypA inhibitors on viral DNA replication and early (e.g., p30) and late viral expression (p72 and other late proteins) in single-cycle assays.
- Mechanism of Cyp A action on p72 stability. Beyond p72 stabilization, it remains unclear whether CypA acts as a chaperone for proper p72 folding and trimerization. Can the authors determine if p72 trimers are formed in CypA knockout cells, with or without co-expression of pB602L?
- K63-linked ubiquitination. The claim in the Abstract that ´interaction with CypA stabilizes p72 by reducing K63-linked ubiquitination and preventing proteasomal degradation` appears overstated. This conclusion is based solely on overexpression assays in transfected cells lacking pB602, which is essential for proper p72 folding and trimerization (indeed, ´expression of p72 alone leads to the formation of misfolded p72 aggregates`; refs. 11, 13, 16). Moreover, K63-linked ubiquitination is typically associated with signaling rather than degradation. The authors should temper this conclusion and contextualize the limitations of their system, especially as it differs markedly from the infection setting.
- p72 immunofluorescence patterns. The intracellular distribution of p72 in infected cells (Figs. 2F and 8F) appears diffuse and, surprisingly, largely excluded from assembly sites, which is inconsistent with that expected for the major capsid protein. This contrasts with established reports showing p72 localization to viral factories and cytoplasmic puncta corresponding to scattered virions. This discrepancy undermines claims about colocalization with CypA (Fig. 2F) and the late virion protein p54 (Fig. 8F), and should be addressed.
Other Points
- In Fig. 6, CypA inhibitors appear to suppress ASFV replication more strongly than CypA knockdown. What accounts for this difference? Would similar results be observed in CypA knockout cells?
- The work does not analyse if p72-Cyp A interaction persists upon ASFV assembly. This would be relevant, as retention of p72-Cyp A complexes in virions could influence early replication events after infection.
- In Fig. 8, the low viral production in the control factories (DMSO) is striking. Is this representative of PAM infections with ASFV strain HLJ/18? The reduction in factory size in the presence of CypA inhibitors also does not appear as significant as in the graphs.
- Viral genome quantification alone does not distinguish between infectious and non-infectious particles. A viral titration assay should be performed to assess the actual impact on infectivity.
- Fig. 2A shows an unexplained band between GST and GST– CypA. Is this a degradation product or a contaminant? Clarification is needed.
- The Discussion lacks depth and does not contextualize the findings against prior literature, particularly regarding the phenotypic consequences of p72 and pB602 abrogation. It also misses the opportunity to compare and discuss the broader roles of CypA in the life cycles of other viruses (e.g., HIV, SARS-CoV-2, IBV, etc).
- References: Literature citations are sometimes not accurate enough, and self-citations are sometimes overused. For instance:
· Line 56–57 cites one relevant reference (own) on p72’s role in capsid formation and viral assembly (Wang et al. 2019. Science), omitting two other relevant cryo-EM studies on ASFV structure (Liu et al. 2019. Cell Host & Microbe, and Andres et al. 2019. J Biol Chem), and a significant structural analysis of p72 capsomers (Liu et al., Cell Res, 2019). It would be fair to acknowledge the work of other researchers as well.
·Line 54–56 attributes p72 abundance data to Ref. 8, when it was actually reported in Andrés et al. (J Virol, 1997, 71:2331). Please correct
· The use of self-reference 5 on ´promising p15 immunogen` to support general statements about the lack of antiviral therapies (lines 47–49) and self-reference 17 to support late p72 expression (already well-established) appears unnecessary.
